We require, an electronic balance, starch powder, butter paper, dropper, spatula, glass rod, pestle and mortar, distilled water, beakers, wire gauze, tripod stand, Bunsen burner, funnel, filter paper, conical flask, iron stand with clamp etc.
Weigh 1 gm of starch using a weighing balance.
Put the weighed starch in a mortar and add few ml of distilled water into it using a dropper.
Grind the starch with a pestle to make a thin paste.
Transfer this paste to a 50 ml beaker.
Transfer this paste to a 50 ml beaker.
Transfer this paste to a 50 ml beaker.
Heat distilled water in a 250ml beaker.
Take about 100 ml of distilled water in a 250 ml beaker and heat the beaker so that the water starts boiling.
Pour the paste slowly into the boiling water with stirring using a glass rod.
Continue boiling for about 10 minutes and then allow the beaker to cool.
Fix a filter paper in a funnel which is fixed to a stand and place a glass rod over the funnel.
Filter the contents of the beaker through the funnel and collect the filtrate in a conical flask. 5.
Label the filtrate “Starch Sol”.
Take the starch sol containing sodium chloride in a conical flask.
Take a parchment membrane.
And fix it on to the stem of the funnel.
Using a thread, tie it to the end of the stem of the funnel.
Pour the Starch sol containing Sodium chloride into the parchment bag through the funnel till two-thirds of the bag is full.
Pour the Starch sol containing Sodium chloride into the parchment bag through the funnel till two-thirds of the bag is full.
Dip the parchment bag into distilled water taken in a beaker and fix the funnel in position by means of the clamp.
Dip the parchment bag into distilled water taken in a beaker and fix the funnel in position by means of the clamp.
Allow it to stand for about half an hour.
Take 1 ml of water from the beaker using a dropper.
Transfer it into a test tube.
Take small quantity of iodine solution using a dropper.
Add few drops of iodine solution into the test tube containing water. If the colour does not turn blue, it depicts the absence of starch in water.
To this add a few drops of iodine solution. (If no blue color appears, it depicts absence of starch in water.)
Withdraw another 1 ml of water from the beaker.
Transfer into another test tube.
To this add a few drops of Silver nitrate (AgNO[sub]3[/sub]) solution.
To this add a few drops of Silver nitrate (AgNO[sub]3[/sub]) solution.
A white precipitate is produced immediately. (This indicates the presence of chloride ions and hence confirms the sodium chloride in water).
A white precipitate is produced immediately. (This indicates the presences of Chloride ions and hence the presence of sodium chloride in water).
It follows that sodium and chloride ions diffuse through the parchment membrane. As sodium ion and chloride ion diffuse out of the starch sol, it gets free from ions gradually.
Replace the water in the beaker with fresh distilled water.
After about 10 minutes, test the presence of chloride ions.
Continue the test for the presence of Chloride ions.
Continue the test for the presence of Chloride ions.
Continue the test for the presence of Chloride ions.
If no white precipitate is formed, chloride ions are absent.

We require an egg, beakers, glass rod, 5% NaCl solution, filter paper, funnel, conical flask, iron stand with clamp.
Take an egg.
Break the outer shell of the egg by striking it with a glass rod.
Break the shell of the egg using a glass rod.
Collect the colorless liquid (Egg albumin) along with the yellow yolk in a beaker.
Decant the colorless liquid (Egg albumin) into another beaker.
Transfer the egg albumin into a beaker containing 5% NaCl solution.
Transfer the egg albumin into a beaker containing 5% NaCl solution.
Stir it constantly for about 15-20 minutes.
Place a filter paper in a funnel which is fixed on a stand.
Filter the contents of the beaker through the funnel and collect it in a conical flask.
Label the filtrate “Egg-albumin Sol”.

We require, 2% solution of aluminium chloride, silver nitrate solution, dropper, glass rod, distilled water, beakers, wire gauze, tripod stand, Bunsen burner, funnel, filter paper, conical flask, parchment membrane, iron stand with clamp etc.
Take a 250 ml conical flask and clean it by the steaming-out process.

Boil the water.
Take some Aluminum chloride solution into a dropper.
Add it dropwise into the boiling water.
Continue boiling until a deep red/ brown solution (Aluminum hydroxide) is obtained.
Keep the contents of the conical flask undisturbed for some time at room temperature. Label the solution as "Aluminum Hydroxide sol".

We require, solid arseniuos oxide, hydrogen sulphide gas, Distilled water, conical flask, beakers, RB flask, glass rod, glass tube, flutted filter paper, wire gauze, tripod stand, Bunsen burner, kipp’s apparatus, iron stand with clamp etc.
Clean a 250 ml conical flask by steaming out process.
Clean a 250 ml conical flask by steaming out process.
Clean a 250 ml conical flask by steaming out process.
Take the cleaned conical flask.
Take the cleaned conical flask.
To this cleaned flask, add 0.2 g of arsenious oxide.
To this cleaned flask, add 0.2 g of arsenious oxide.
Take 100 ml of distilled water in a measuring jar.
Add 150-200 ml of distilled water to the solid using a measuring cylinder.
Boil the solution for about 10 minutes.
Boil the solution with stirring for about 10 minutes by placing the flask over the Bunsen burner. Arsenious oxide undergoes hydrolysis with boiling distilled water to form arsenous acid.

Arsenous acid reacts with hydrogen sulphide to form yellow coloured arsenious sulphide. Continue passing hydrogen sulphide gas till the intensity of colour does not change further.
